Outlandish
owt-LAN-dish
adjective
From the Old English ūtlendisc, “of a foreign land,” from ūt (“out”) and land; hence foreign, of another country. The modern sense of “bizarre” is a later drift; in the KJV it means simply foreign.

Biblical Definition

Outlandish in the KJV does not mean strange or absurd, as our ears now take it. It means of an out-land — foreign, belonging to another country. It occurs once, in Nehemiah’s hardest reproof. He had found men of Judah who had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, whose children could not speak the Jews’ language, and he contended with them and pressed the case with the one example none could answer: “Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God… nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin” (Neh 13:26). The argument is devastating. Solomon was the wisest of men, beloved of his God, unmatched among kings — and his foreign wives turned away his heart after other gods, so that his heart was not perfect with the LORD (1Ki 11:4). If wisdom itself could be dragged into idolatry through the marriage bed, what shall become of lesser men? Nehemiah’s charge is named plainly: “to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives” (Neh 13:27). It is a covenant question, not a blood question. The danger of the outlandish wife was never her ancestry but her altar — she brought Chemosh and Ashtoreth into the house, and the husband bowed. Paul says the same to the church in the language of the yoke: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers… what communion hath light with darkness?” (2Co 6:14). The line God draws runs between faith and unbelief, and it has never run between peoples.

Webster 1828 Definition

Foreign; of another land. In the KJV the plain sense is foreign, not the modern “bizarre.”

OUTLANDISH, foreign; belonging to another country; not native.

From Old English ūtlendisc, “of an out-land.”

The modern sense of “bizarre, absurd” is a later drift of the word.

A KJV hapax: outlandish women caused Solomon to sin (Neh 13:26).

Nehemiah names the sin as marrying strange wives against the covenant (Neh 13:27).

Key Scripture

Neh 13:26 — "Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel: nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin."

Neh 13:27 — "Shall we then hearken unto you to do all this great evil, to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives?"

2Co 6:14 — "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

Rut 1:16 — "And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:"

Modern Corruption

The KJV word for foreign; it recovers Nehemiah’s warning against the unequal yoke — a covenant matter, never a matter of blood or nation.

expand to see more

The live corruption here is the abuse of Nehemiah’s text for ethnic separatism, and it must be named and refused outright. Men have taken “outlandish women” and the strange wives of Ezra and Nehemiah and made of them a charter for keeping the peoples apart by blood — as though God’s objection to Solomon’s wives were their ancestry. It was not. It was their altars. “His wives turned away his heart after other gods,” and Nehemiah names the sin exactly: “to transgress against our God in marrying strange wives.” Scripture’s own witnesses settle it. Ruth was a Moabitess and is in the line of David and of Christ, because she said, “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” Rahab was a Canaanite of Jericho and is named in the genealogy and in the roll of faith. The daughters of Moab were not shut out by blood; they were shut out by Chemosh, and when a Moabitess renounced Chemosh she was a daughter of Israel. Biblical anthropology knows two families only: one in Adam, where all fell, and one in Christ, where there is neither Jew nor Greek. Any reading that makes nation or lineage the boundary of the covenant is a corruption of the text it quotes.

The principle to recover, then, is the unequal yoke as Scripture actually draws it — between faith and unbelief, light and darkness, Christ and Belial. Solomon is the warning God chose: wisest of men, beloved of his God, unequalled among kings, and his heart was turned by the women he loved until it was not perfect with the LORD. If him, then whom? A believer who marries an unbeliever has not merely chosen a hard road; he has yoked his soul to an altar not his own and given his children a mother or a father who will teach them another god. The rule is not that a Christian must marry his own kind of people. The rule is that he must marry in the Lord — and by that rule a Moabitess who fears the LORD is a fitter wife than a daughter of Judah who does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means foreign, of another land — the KJV sense, older than the modern “bizarre.”

expand to see more

Outlandish — Old English ūtlendisc, “of a foreign land.”

From ūt (“out”) + land; hence not native, foreign.

The modern sense “bizarre” is a drift; the KJV means only foreign.

A KJV hapax: outlandish women caused Solomon to sin (Neh 13:26).

The offence was the altar, not the ancestry — strange gods, not strange blood.

Usage

"Outlandish means foreign, not absurd: the outlandish women of Neh 13 were wives of other lands."

"Even Solomon, wisest of men, was turned by outlandish wives — the yoke bends the strongest neck."

"Ruth the Moabitess was outlandish by birth and a daughter of Israel by faith: the altar draws the line."
